questions.question: Q: What is the difference between a use-by date and a best-before date?

points.text: A use-by date is about safety — food should not be eaten after this date. A best-before date is about quality — food may still be safe to eat after this date but may not be at its best.

questions.question: Q: What do the three colours in the traffic light labelling system mean?

points.text: Green = low (healthier choice), amber = moderate, red = high (eat less often or in smaller amounts). They apply to fat, saturated fat, sugars, and salt.

questions.question: Q: List four of the 14 major allergens that must be declared on food labels.

points.text: Celery, cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs, mustard, nuts, peanuts, sesame, soybeans, sulphur dioxide (any four).

questions.question: Q: What must a product contain to be labelled 'low fat'?

points.text: No more than 3g of fat per 100g of the product.

questions.question: Q: Why can food marketing be misleading? Give an example.

points.text: Marketing focuses on positive aspects while downplaying negatives. Example: a 'low fat' yoghurt may be high in sugar; 'no added sugar' does not mean the product is sugar-free.

questions.question: Q: What seven nutrients must be shown on nutritional information labels?

points.text: Energy (kJ/kcal), fat, saturated fat, carbohydrate, sugars, protein, and salt.

questions.question: Q: In what order must ingredients be listed on a food label?

points.text: In descending order by weight — the ingredient present in the largest amount is listed first.

questions.question: Q: What is the Reference Intake (RI) on a food label?

points.text: The RI shows the recommended maximum daily amount of key nutrients for an average adult, helping consumers understand how a product fits into their daily diet.
